title: About
text:
The Public Record is a starter publication for evidence-led investigations of public data. Its central rule is simple: a reader should be able to trace every published claim back to a source and inspect every consequential transformation.
The finished article is only one view of the work. The repository also preserves the source snapshot, retrieval details, cleaning and analysis code, assumptions, limitations, and revision history.

title: About
text:
Contact and corrections
Corrections can be proposed through the public GitHub repository. A correction should identify what changed, when it changed, and whether the change affected the article’s conclusions. Material corrections belong both on the article and in the repository history.

title: The long slowdown in U.S. population growth
text:
What we asked
How has the pace of United States population growth changed over the period covered by the World Bank’s annual population series?
This is intentionally a small example. Its job is to demonstrate the publication structure: a reader can inspect the preserved API response, run the transformation script, download the resulting table, and see the analytical code used in the article.

title: The long slowdown in U.S. population growth
text:
What the data shows
The U.S. population increased over the full series, but the annual rate of growth did not move in a straight line. The chart below lets readers inspect the level and year-over-year change separately.


Show the complete chart code
population = FileAttachment("data/processed/us_population.csv").csv({typed: true})

Plot.plot({
  width: 850,
  height: 430,
  marginLeft: 70,
  y: {grid: true, label: "Population"},
  x: {label: null, ticks: 10, tickFormat: d => String(d)},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0]),
    Plot.lineY(population, {x: "year", y: "population", stroke: "#136f63", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(population, {x: "year", y: "population", fill: "#136f63", r: 2.5}),
    Plot.tip(population, Plot.pointerX({
      x: "year",
      y: "population",
      title: d => `${d.year}: ${d.population.toLocaleString()}`
    }))
  ]
})


















Show the annual-growth chart code
growth = population.filter(d => d.annual_growth_pct !== null && !Number.isNaN(d.annual_growth_pct))

Plot.plot({
  width: 850,
  height: 390,
  marginLeft: 60,
  y: {grid: true, label: "Annual growth (%)"},
  x: {label: null, ticks: 10, tickFormat: d => String(d)},
  color: {legend: false},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#8c8c8c"}),
    Plot.barY(growth, {
      x: "year",
      y: "annual_growth_pct",
      fill: d => d.annual_growth_pct >= 1 ? "#136f63" : "#d9903d"
    }),
    Plot.tip(growth, Plot.pointerX({
      x: "year",
      y: "annual_growth_pct",
      title: d => `${d.year}: ${d.annual_growth_pct.toFixed(2)}%`
    }))
  ]
})
















The purpose of this demonstration is not to assign a cause. Population change reflects births, deaths, and migration, and this one series does not separate them. A responsible causal investigation would add those components and examine revisions and uncertainty in the underlying estimates.

title: The long slowdown in U.S. population growth
text:
Methodology
The retrieval script calls the World Bank Indicators API for SP.POP.TOTL and the country code USA. The raw JSON response is preserved byte-for-byte. The transformation script:

verifies the expected response structure and indicator identifier;
removes observations with no value;
converts year and population to integers;
sorts observations in ascending year order; and
calculates year-over-year percentage change as (current / previous - 1) × 100.

No observations are manually added, removed, or edited. The processed CSV can be regenerated without network access:
python3 investigations/us-population-growth/scripts/analyze.py
To deliberately fetch a new source snapshot and then rebuild the analysis:
python3 investigations/us-population-growth/scripts/fetch_data.py
python3 investigations/us-population-growth/scripts/analyze.py

title: The long slowdown in U.S. population growth
text:
Limitations

This is a descriptive series, not a causal model.
The World Bank may revise historical observations; the committed snapshot is therefore part of the evidence.
The series is annual and cannot describe within-year changes.
A national total can conceal substantial differences between places and groups.
Growth calculated from rounded published values may differ slightly from a publisher’s separately calculated rate.

text:
Sources
World Bank, Population, total — United States, indicator SP.POP.TOTL, retrieved through the World Bank Indicators API. Series definitions and metadata are available on the World Bank indicator page.

Reproducible outputs. A single documented command rebuilds derived data and the site.

title: How we work
text:
Evidence hierarchy
Primary government and institutional sources are preferred. Mirrors and aggregators may aid discovery, but the article should link to the originating publisher whenever possible. A source’s official status does not make it error-free; definitions, revisions, collection methods, and known limitations still require scrutiny.

title: How we work
text:
Reproduction levels
Each article declares one of these levels:

Fully reproducible: all necessary inputs and code are included or openly downloadable.
Reproducible with external data: code is complete, but a documented download is required because data is too large to commit.
Partially reproducible: a legal, privacy, or access constraint prevents redistribution; the missing component and verification approach are stated prominently.

The example investigation in this starter is fully reproducible from its committed snapshot. Refreshing the snapshot requires internet access, but reproducing the published result does not.

title: How we work
text:
Corrections policy
Silent substantive edits are not acceptable. Typographical fixes may rely on Git history; factual or analytical changes should add a dated correction note explaining the original statement, the change, and its effect on the conclusion.
